title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 248
paragraphs: Of the account given by Etearchus the Ammonian let this much suffice, except that, as the men of Cyrene told me, he claimed the Nasamonians returned safely home, and that the people to whom they had come were all wizards. Now Etearchus conjectured this river running past the city to be the Nile; and reason compels us to think so. For the Nile flows from Libya and cuts Libya through the middle; and as I conjecture, judging of what is not known by what is evident to the view, it sets out at a distance from its mouth equal to that of the Ister. For the river Ister begins from the country of the Celts and the city of Pyrene, and so runs that it divides Europe through the middle (the Celts are outside the Pillars of Heracles and border upon the Cynesians, who dwell furthest towards the sunset of all peoples in Europe); and the Ister ends, after running through the whole of Europe, by flowing into the Euxine Sea at the place where the Milesians have their settlement of Istria.
